title: Chapter 32 — Cetology
paragraphs: Already we are boldly launched upon the deep. But soon we shall be lost in its shoreless, harborless vastness. Before that happens — before the Pequod's weedy hull rolls alongside the barnacled hulls of whales — it would be wise at the outset to attend to a matter almost essential for a thorough understanding of the many whale-related revelations and references that are to follow.

What I want to put before you is a systematic overview of the whale in his broad categories. Yet this is no easy task. What I am attempting here is nothing less than the classification of chaos. Listen to what the best and most recent authorities have said.
"No branch of Zoology is so confused as that which is called Cetology," says Captain Scoresby, 1820.

"It is not my intention, were it in my power, to inquire into the true method of dividing the cetacea into groups and families. Utter confusion exists among the historians of this animal" (the sperm whale), says Surgeon Beale, 1839.

"Unfitness to pursue our research in the unfathomable waters." "Impenetrable veil covering our knowledge of the cetacea." "A field strewn with thorns." "All these incomplete indications but serve to torture us naturalists."

So speak the great Cuvier, John Hunter, and Lesson — those lights of zoology and anatomy. Nevertheless, though real knowledge is scarce, books are plentiful. And so it is, to some small degree, with cetology, the science of whales. Many men, small and great, old and new, landsmen and seamen, have written about the whale at length or in brief. Let me run over a few: the authors of the Bible; Aristotle; Pliny; Aldrovandi; Sir Thomas Browne; Gesner; Ray; Linnaeus; Rondeletius; Willoughby; Green; Artedi; Sibbald; Brisson; Marten; Lacepede; Bonneterre; Desmarest; Baron Cuvier; Frederick Cuvier; John Hunter; Owen; Scoresby; Beale; Bennett; J. Ross Browne; the author of Miriam Coffin; Olmstead; and the Reverend T. Cheever. But to what useful generalizing purpose all these have written, the extracts cited above will show.

Of the names on this list of whale authors, only those after Owen ever saw a living whale. And only one of them was an actual professional harpooner and whaleman. I mean Captain Scoresby. On the specific subject of the Greenland or right whale, he is the best authority available. But Scoresby knew nothing and said nothing about the great sperm whale, compared to which the Greenland whale is almost not worth mentioning. And let it be said here that the Greenland whale is a pretender to the throne of the seas. He is not even close to being the largest of the whales. Yet, because his claims go back so far, and because of the profound ignorance that, until some seventy years ago, surrounded the then mythical or completely unknown sperm whale — an ignorance that to this day still prevails everywhere except in a few scientific circles and whaling ports — this usurpation has been total. Check nearly all the whale references in the great poets of the past, and you'll find that the Greenland whale, without a rival, was their monarch of the seas. But the time has finally come for a new proclamation. Hear ye, hear ye, good people all — the Greenland whale is dethroned — the great sperm whale now reigns!

There are only two books in existence that claim to present the living sperm whale and actually succeed to any degree. Those are Beale's and Bennett's. Both authors were surgeons on English South Sea whale ships, and both are accurate, reliable men. The original material about the sperm whale in their volumes is necessarily small, but what there is of it is excellent in quality, though mostly limited to scientific description. As yet, however, the sperm whale — whether scientific or poetic — lives complete in no literature. Far above all other hunted whales, his is an unwritten life.

Now the various species of whales need some sort of popular, comprehensive classification, if only a rough outline for now, to be filled in later by others. Since no better person steps forward, I offer my own humble efforts. I promise nothing complete, because anything human that claims to be complete must, for that very reason, be flawed. I won't attempt detailed anatomical descriptions of the various species — not here, at least — or much description of any kind. My goal is simply to sketch out a system of cetology. I am the architect, not the builder.

But it is a weighty task. No ordinary mail sorter at the Post Office is equal to it. To grope down to the bottom of the sea after these creatures, to have one's hands among the unspeakable foundations, ribs, and very pelvis of the world — this is a fearful thing. Who am I to try to hook this leviathan by the nose! The terrifying challenges in the Book of Job might well unnerve me: "Will he make a covenant with thee? Behold, the hope of him is in vain!" But I have swum through libraries and sailed through oceans. I have handled whales with these very hands. I am serious, and I will try. First, some preliminaries to settle.

First: The uncertain, unsettled state of this science of Cetology is demonstrated right at the door by the fact that in some quarters it is still debated whether a whale is a fish. In his System of Nature, 1776, Linnaeus declares: "I hereby separate the whales from the fish." But from my own knowledge, I know that as recently as 1850, sharks and shad and herring were still found sharing the same seas with whales, in defiance of Linnaeus's decree.

The grounds on which Linnaeus would have banished the whales from the waters are these: "On account of their warm, two-chambered heart, their lungs, their movable eyelids, their hollow ears," and their reproductive and nursing anatomy, and finally, "by the law of nature, justly and deservedly." I submitted all this to my friends Simeon Macey and Charley Coffin, both Nantucketers and my former shipmates, and they agreed that the reasons given were altogether insufficient. Charley bluntly called them nonsense.

Let it be known that, setting aside all argument, I take the good old-fashioned position that the whale is a fish, and I call on holy Jonah to back me up. With this fundamental point settled, the next question is: in what internal way does the whale differ from other fish? Linnaeus has given you the details above. But in brief, they are these: lungs and warm blood, whereas all other fish are lungless and cold-blooded.

Next: how shall we define the whale by his obvious external features, so as to label him unmistakably for all time? To be brief, then: a whale is a spouting fish with a horizontal tail. There you have him. However condensed, that definition is the result of careful thought. A walrus spouts much like a whale, but the walrus is not a fish because he is amphibious. The last part of the definition is even more decisive when paired with the first. Almost anyone has noticed that all fish familiar to landlubbers have not a flat but a vertical — that is, an up-and-down — tail. Whereas among spouting fish, the tail, though it may be similarly shaped, always assumes a horizontal position.

By this definition of what a whale is, I do not exclude from the whale brotherhood any sea creature previously identified as a whale by the best-informed Nantucketers. Nor, on the other hand, do I include any fish previously considered to be something else. Hence, all the smaller spouting, horizontal-tailed fish must be included in this plan of Cetology. Now, then, come the grand divisions of the entire whale family.

I am aware that to this day, the fish called Manatees and Dugongs (Pig-fish and Sow-fish to the Coffins of Nantucket) are classified by many naturalists among the whales. But since these pig-fish are a noisy, contemptible lot, mostly lurking in river mouths and feeding on wet hay, and especially since they do not spout, I deny their credentials as whales and have given them their passports to leave the Kingdom of Cetology.
First: according to size, I divide the whales into three primary BOOKS (subdivided into CHAPTERS), which shall include them all, both small and large.
I. THE FOLIO WHALE; II. THE OCTAVO WHALE; III. THE DUODECIMO WHALE.
As the type of the FOLIO I present the Sperm Whale; of the OCTAVO, the Grampus; of the DUODECIMO, the Porpoise.

FOLIOS. Under this heading I include the following chapters: I. The Sperm Whale; II. The Right Whale; III. The Fin-Back Whale; IV. The Humpbacked Whale; V. The Razor Back Whale; VI. The Sulphur Bottom Whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER I (Sperm Whale). — This whale, known vaguely by the old English as the Trumpa whale, the Physeter whale, and the Anvil-Headed whale, is the present Cachalot of the French and the Pottfisch of the Germans. He is, without doubt, the largest inhabitant of the globe, the most formidable of all whales to encounter, the most majestic in appearance, and by far the most valuable commercially — being the only creature from which that precious substance, spermaceti, is obtained. All his peculiarities will be discussed at length elsewhere. For now, it is chiefly his name that concerns me. Considered linguistically, it is absurd. Centuries ago, when the sperm whale was almost completely unknown as an individual species, and his oil was only accidentally obtained from stranded specimens, spermaceti was popularly supposed to come from the creature then known in England as the Greenland or Right Whale. The idea was also that this spermaceti was a certain fluid of the Greenland Whale, which the first syllable of the word literally expresses. In those days, spermaceti was extremely rare, used not for light but only as an ointment and medicine. It could only be bought from druggists, the way you might buy an ounce of rhubarb today. When, as I believe, the true nature of spermaceti eventually became known, its original name was kept by the dealers — no doubt to inflate its value with an air of exotic rarity. And so the name must at last have been transferred to the whale from which this spermaceti actually came.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER II (Right Whale). — In one respect this is the most venerable of all whales, being the first to be regularly hunted by man. It produces the substance commonly known as whalebone or baleen, and the oil known as "whale oil," an inferior product commercially. Among fishermen, he goes by all the following names: The Whale; the Greenland Whale; the Black Whale; the Great Whale; the True Whale; the Right Whale. There is considerable confusion about the identity of the species so multiply baptized. What, then, is the whale I include as the second species of my Folios? It is the Great Mysticetus of the English naturalists, the Greenland Whale of the English whalemen, the Baleine Ordinaire of the French whalemen, and the Gronlands Walfish of the Swedes. It is the whale that for more than two centuries has been hunted by the Dutch and English in the Arctic seas, and the whale that American fishermen have long pursued in the Indian Ocean, on the Brazil Banks, on the Northwest Coast, and various other parts of the world designated by them as Right Whale Cruising Grounds.

Some claim to see a difference between the Greenland whale of the English and the right whale of the Americans. But they agree precisely in all their major features, and no one has yet presented a single definitive fact on which to base a real distinction. It is by endless subdivisions based on the most inconclusive differences that some branches of natural history become so repulsively complicated. The right whale will be discussed elsewhere at length, in connection with the sperm whale.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER III (Fin-Back). — Under this heading I count a monster known by various names — Fin-Back, Tall-Spout, and Long-John — seen in almost every sea. This is commonly the whale whose distant spout is so often spotted by passengers crossing the Atlantic on New York packet ships. In length and in his baleen, the Fin-Back resembles the right whale, but is less stout in girth and lighter in color, approaching olive. His great lips have a cable-like look, formed by interlocking, slanting folds of large wrinkles. His distinguishing feature, the fin from which he gets his name, is often easy to spot — some three or four feet long, growing vertically from the rear of his back, angular in shape and sharp-pointed. Even when no other part of the creature is visible, this lone fin will sometimes be seen projecting clearly from the surface. When the sea is moderately calm and slightly rippled, and this fin stands up casting shadows on the wrinkled surface, the surrounding circle of water somewhat resembles a sundial, with its pointer and wavy hour-lines etched upon it. The Fin-Back is not social. He seems a whale-hater, as some men are misanthropes. Very shy — always solitary — rising unexpectedly to the surface in the most remote and desolate waters. His straight, single, tall spout rises like a misanthropic spear on a barren plain. Gifted with such wondrous power and speed in swimming as to defy all human pursuit, this whale seems the banished and unconquerable Cain of his race, bearing as his mark that fin upon his back. Because he has baleen in his mouth, the Fin-Back is sometimes grouped with the right whale among a theoretical class called Whalebone Whales — that is, whales with baleen. Of these so-called Whalebone Whales, there appear to be several varieties, most of them poorly known: broad-nosed whales, beaked whales, pike-headed whales, bunched whales, under-jawed whales, and rostrated whales, to give the fishermen's names for a few.

Regarding the name "Whalebone Whales," it is important to note that while such a term is convenient for referring to a certain kind of whale, it is useless to try to classify whales based on their baleen, hump, fin, or teeth, even though those features might seem the most obvious basis for a system. The problem is this: baleen, hump, back-fin, and teeth are features distributed randomly among all sorts of whales, with no regard for the nature of their other, more essential characteristics. The sperm whale and the humpback whale both have a hump, but there the resemblance ends. The humpback whale and the Greenland whale both have baleen, but again the resemblance ends. And it's the same with the other features listed above. Among the various species of whales, they form such irregular combinations — or, taken individually, such random occurrences — that they completely defy any orderly system based on them. On this rock every whale-naturalist has wrecked.

But perhaps, you might think, in the whale's internal parts — his anatomy — there we could find the right classification. Not so. What feature of the Greenland whale's anatomy is more striking than his baleen? Yet we've seen that baleen is useless for classification. And if you look inside the various whales, you'll find distinctions a fiftieth as useful to the classifier as the external ones already listed. What remains? Nothing but to take hold of the whales physically, in their full liberal volume, and sort them boldly by size. And this is the bibliographical system I adopt here. It is the only one that can possibly work, for it alone is practical. Let us proceed.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER IV (Humpback). — This whale is often seen off the northern American coast. He has been frequently captured there and towed into harbor. He carries a great hump on his back like a peddler's pack — you might call him the pack-horse whale. In any case, his popular name doesn't sufficiently distinguish him, since the sperm whale also has a hump, though a smaller one. His oil is not very valuable. He has baleen. He is the most playful and lighthearted of all the whales, making more joyful foam and white water than any other.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER V (Razor Back). — Of this whale, little is known but his name. I have seen him at a distance off Cape Horn. Of a retiring nature, he eludes both hunters and scholars. Though no coward, he has never shown any part of himself but his back, which rises in a long, sharp ridge. Let him go. I know little more of him, and neither does anyone else.

BOOK I (Folio), CHAPTER VI (Sulphur Bottom). — Another shy gentleman, with a yellow belly, doubtless acquired by scraping along the ocean floor in some of his deepest dives. He is seldom seen — at least I have never seen him except in the remote southern seas, and always at too great a distance to study his appearance. He is never chased — he would run off with whole warehouses of rope. Amazing things are told about him. Farewell, Sulphur Bottom! I can say nothing more that is true of you, and neither can the oldest Nantucketer.
Thus ends BOOK I (Folio), and now begins BOOK II (Octavo).
OCTAVOES. — These include the whales of middling size, among which we may count: I. The Grampus; II. The Blackfish; III. The Narwhal; IV. The Thrasher; V. The Killer.

Why this book of whales is not called the Quarto is quite obvious. While the whales of this order, though smaller than the Folios, retain a proportionate resemblance to them in shape, the bookbinder's quarto volume does not preserve the shape of the folio, but the octavo does.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER I (Grampus). — Though this fish, whose loud, sonorous breathing has supplied a proverb for landlubbers, is a well-known resident of the deep, he is not popularly classified among whales. But possessing all the grand distinctive features of the whale, most naturalists have recognized him as one. He is moderate octavo size, ranging from fifteen to twenty-five feet in length, with corresponding girth. He swims in herds. He is never regularly hunted, though his oil is considerable in quantity and fairly good for light. Some fishermen regard his appearance as a sign that the great sperm whale is approaching.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER II (Blackfish). — I use the popular fishermen's names for all these fish, as they are generally the best. When any name happens to be vague or misleading, I will say so and suggest another. I do so now with the Blackfish, so called, because blackness is the rule among almost all whales. So call him the Hyena Whale, if you prefer. His voracity is well known, and because the inner angles of his lips curve upward, he wears an everlasting devilish grin on his face. This whale averages sixteen to eighteen feet in length and is found in almost all latitudes. He has a peculiar way of showing his hooked dorsal fin while swimming, which looks something like a Roman nose. When not more profitably employed, sperm whale hunters sometimes capture the Hyena Whale to maintain a supply of cheap oil for domestic use — as some thrifty housekeepers, in the absence of company, burn smelly tallow instead of fragrant wax. Though their blubber is very thin, some of these whales will yield upwards of thirty gallons of oil.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER III (Narwhal), that is, Nostril Whale. — Another curiously named whale, so called I suppose because his peculiar horn was originally mistaken for a pointed nose. The creature is about sixteen feet long, while its horn averages five feet, though some exceed ten and even reach fifteen feet. Strictly speaking, this horn is an elongated tusk growing out from the jaw at a slightly downward angle. But it only grows from the left side, which gives its owner a look somewhat like a clumsy left-handed man. What purpose this ivory horn or lance serves is hard to say. It doesn't seem to be used like the blades of the swordfish or billfish, though some sailors tell me the narwhal uses it as a rake for turning over the sea bottom for food. Charley Coffin said it was used as an ice-piercer: the narwhal, rising to the surface of the polar sea and finding it covered with ice, thrusts his horn up and breaks through. But you can't prove either theory correct. My own opinion is that, however the narwhal actually uses his one-sided horn, it would certainly be very convenient as a bookmark for reading pamphlets. The narwhal has also been called the Tusked Whale, the Horned Whale, and the Unicorn Whale. He is certainly a curious example of the unicorn idea found in almost every kingdom of nature. From certain old authors I have learned that this sea-unicorn's horn was in ancient times believed to be a great antidote against poison, and preparations of it fetched enormous prices. It was also distilled into smelling salts for fainting ladies, much as deer antlers are made into hartshorn. Originally it was considered a great curiosity in itself. Old accounts tell me that Sir Martin Frobisher, on his return from a voyage, when Queen Elizabeth waved her jeweled hand to him from a window of Greenwich Palace as his bold ship sailed down the Thames — "when Sir Martin returned from that voyage," the old records say, "on bended knee he presented to Her Highness a prodigious long horn of the narwhal, which for a long period hung in Windsor Castle." An Irish author claims that the Earl of Leicester, also on bended knee, presented to Her Highness another horn, belonging to a land beast of the unicorn variety.

The narwhal has a very picturesque, leopard-like appearance, being milk-white with round and oblong spots of black. His oil is very fine and clear, but there is little of it, and he is seldom hunted. He is mostly found in the Arctic seas.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER IV (Killer). — Of this whale, the Nantucketer knows little with certainty, and the professional naturalist knows nothing at all. From what I have seen of him at a distance, I would say he is about the size of a grampus. He is very savage — a sort of cannibal fish. He sometimes seizes great Folio whales by the lip and hangs there like a leech until the mighty brute is worried to death. The Killer is never hunted. I have never heard what sort of oil he has. His name might be objected to on the grounds of vagueness. For we are all killers, on land and on sea — Napoleons and sharks included.

BOOK II (Octavo), CHAPTER V (Thrasher). — This gentleman is famous for his tail, which he uses like a rod for whipping his enemies. He mounts the Folio whale's back and, as he swims, works his passage by flogging him — as some schoolmasters get through the world by a similar method. Even less is known about the Thrasher than the Killer. Both are outlaws, even in the lawless seas.
Thus ends BOOK II (Octavo), and begins BOOK III (Duodecimo).
DUODECIMOS. — These include the smaller whales: I. The Huzza Porpoise. II. The Algerine Porpoise. III. The Mealy-Mouthed Porpoise.

To those who haven't studied the subject, it may seem strange that fish commonly no more than four or five feet long should be ranked among WHALES — a word that always carries an idea of hugeness. But the creatures listed above as Duodecimos are undeniably whales, by my definition of what a whale is: a spouting fish with a horizontal tail.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER I (Huzza Porpoise). — This is the common porpoise found almost everywhere on the globe. The name is my own invention, since there are more than one sort of porpoise and something must be done to tell them apart. I call him this because he always swims in cheerful schools that keep tossing themselves skyward like caps in a Fourth of July crowd. Their appearance is generally greeted with delight by sailors. Full of high spirits, they always come from the breezy waves to windward. They are the lads who always live before the wind. They are considered a lucky omen. If you can't manage three cheers at the sight of these lively fish, then heaven help you — the spirit of joyful fun is not in you. A well-fed, plump Huzza Porpoise will yield about one good gallon of oil. But the fine, delicate fluid extracted from his jaws is extremely valuable and sought after by jewelers and watchmakers. Sailors use it on their whetstones. Porpoise meat is good eating, you know. It may never have occurred to you that a porpoise spouts. Indeed, his spout is so small that it's not easily noticed. But next time you have a chance, watch him — and you'll see the great sperm whale himself in miniature.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER II (Algerine Porpoise). — A pirate. Very savage. He is only found, I think, in the Pacific. He is somewhat larger than the Huzza Porpoise but much the same in general build. Provoke him and he'll take on a shark. I've gone after him many times but have never seen one captured.

BOOK III (Duodecimo), CHAPTER III (Mealy-Mouthed Porpoise). — The largest kind of porpoise, found only in the Pacific as far as is known. His only English name is the one given by fishermen — Right-Whale Porpoise — from the fact that he is mainly found near that great whale. In shape he differs somewhat from the Huzza Porpoise, being less round and stout — indeed, quite trim and gentlemanly in figure. He has no fins on his back (most other porpoises do). He has a lovely tail and sentimental hazel eyes with an Indian look. But his mealy mouth ruins everything. Though his entire back down to his side fins is deep black, a boundary line, sharp as the mark on a ship's hull called the "bright waist," streaks him from stem to stern in two separate colors — black above and white below. The white extends over part of his head and his whole mouth, making him look as if he just got caught raiding a flour bag. A most pitiful and mealy appearance! His oil is much like the common porpoise's.

Beyond the DUODECIMO, this system does not go, since the porpoise is the smallest of the whales. Above, you have all the notable Leviathans. But there is a rabble of uncertain, fleeting, half-mythical whales that I, as an American whaleman, know by reputation but not personally. I will list them by their deck-hand names, since such a list may prove valuable to future researchers who may complete what I have only begun. If any of the following whales should be caught and identified, they can easily be added to this system according to their Folio, Octavo, or Duodecimo size: the Bottle-Nose Whale; the Junk Whale; the Pudding-Headed Whale; the Cape Whale; the Leading Whale; the Cannon Whale; the Scragg Whale; the Coppered Whale; the Elephant Whale; the Iceberg Whale; the Quog Whale; the Blue Whale; and so on. From Icelandic, Dutch, and old English sources, other lists of uncertain whales could be quoted, blessed with all manner of outlandish names. But I omit them as completely obsolete, and I can't help suspecting them of being mere words — full of whale-like grandeur but signifying nothing.

Finally: it was stated at the outset that this system would not be perfected here and now. You can plainly see that I have kept my word. But I now leave my cetological system standing unfinished, even as the great Cathedral of Cologne was left, with the crane still standing atop the uncompleted tower. Small structures may be finished by their first builders. Grand ones, true ones, always leave the capstone to posterity. God keep me from ever completing anything. This whole book is but a draft — no, but the draft of a draft. Oh, Time, Strength, Cash, and Patience!
